'''''Malvaviscus arboreus''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[hibiscus]] family, [[Malvaceae]],<ref name="GRIN"/> that is native to the [[American South]],<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=MAAR14 |title=''Malvaviscus arboreus'' Dill. ex Cav. wax mallow |work=PLANTS Database |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=2009-12-16}}</ref> [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], and [[South America]]. The specific name, ''arboreus'', refers to the [[tree]]-like appearance of a mature plant. It is now popular in cultivation<ref name="Clay">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=692L-8HWiEsC |first=Horace F. |last=Clay |author2=James C. Hubbard |title=Tropical Shrubs |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |year=1987 |isbn=978-0-8248-1128-0 |page=104}}</ref> and goes by many English names including '''wax mallow''',  '''Turk's cap''' (mallow), '''Turk's turban''', '''sleeping hibiscus''', '''manzanilla''', '''manzanita''' (de pollo), '''ladies teardrop''' and '''Scotchman's purse'''; many of these common names refer to other, in some cases unrelated, plants. Its [[flower]]s do not open fully and help attract [[Butterfly|butterflies]] and [[hummingbird]]s.

== Distribution ==
''Malvaviscus arboreus'' is native to Central America, Mexico, and the Gulf Coast of the United States, particularly as an understory shrub in coastal Texas and Louisiana.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Turner|first1=Billie L.|last2=Mendenhall|first2=Meghan G.|date=1993|title=A Revision of Malvaviscus (Malvaceae)|journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden|volume=80|issue=2|pages=439–457|doi=10.2307/2399792|issn=0026-6493|jstor=2399792|hdl=2152/31149|s2cid=87867194 |url=https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/bitstream/2152/31149/1/RevisionOfMalvaviscus.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:TurkCap or Scotchman's purse -- Malvaviscus arboreus.jpg|thumb|200px|left|TurkCap or Scotchman's purse -- Malvaviscus arboreus is a flower native to Texas]]
''Malvaviscus arboreus'' is a common understory shrub where it occurs in Texas and is an important food source for female and juvenile Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (''[[Ruby-throated hummingbird|Archilochus colubri]]'') and Black-chinned Hummingbirds (''[[Black-chinned hummingbird|A. alexandri]]''). Each individual flower lasts two days but contains more nectar on the first day.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=George|first=Mary Wissink|date=October 1980|title=Hummingbird foraging behavior at Malvaviscus arboreus var. drummondii|url=https://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v097n04/p0790-p0794.pdf|journal=The Auk|volume=97|issue=4|pages=790–794|doi=10.1093/auk/97.4.790|via=Searchable Ornithological Research Archive}}</ref>

An example occurrence of ''M. arboreus'' is within the coastal Petenes mangroves of the Yucatán region of Mexico, in which plant community it is a subdominant species.<ref>World Wildlife Fund. eds. Mark McGinley, C.Michael Hogan & C. Cleveland. 2010. [http://www.eoearth.org/article/Petenes_mangroves?topic=49597 ''Petenes mangroves''. Encyclopedia of Earth. National Council for Science and the Environment. Washington DC] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111015030054/http://www.eoearth.org/article/Petenes_mangroves?topic=49597 |date=2011-10-15 }}</ref> ''M. arboreus'' is the primary host plant for the [[caterpillar]]s of the Turk's-cap White-Skipper (''[[Heliopetes macaira]]'').<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=2019 |title=Turk's-cap White-Skipper ''Heliopetes macaira'' (Reakirt, [1867]) |publisher=Butterflies and Moths of North America |access-date=2010-08-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100620191404/http://butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=2019 |archive-date=2010-06-20 }}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
''Malvaviscus arboreus'' is commonly cultivated in shady to sunny sites in butterfly and hummingbird gardens across the southern United States.  It can be propagated from fresh seeds or from softwood cuttings.  It often blooms from May through November, but will bloom throughout a mild winter.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=MAARD|title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin|website=www.wildflower.org|access-date=2019-03-27}}</ref>
